fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. Verse 4 says Ahaz sacrificed and burned incense “…on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.” The verse never names the temple at all. This man had more spots than I have cookie cutters, and I used to have six.
Right, baker. The text says Ahaz “…sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.” Those are the places the verse names. The temple isn't one of them.

Hiram, king of Tyre, sends his servants to Solomon in 1 Kings 5:1, which is a different story. In this one, Ahaz sends his messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. Different king, right idea, since Ahaz really is asking another king for help.

You've got it, friend. Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's palace. Then he sent it as a gift to the king of Assyria. Silver and gold from two places, all in one gift.

Horses and chariots? Ooh, fancy, friend, but that's not the list. Verse 8 says Ahaz took silver and gold from the house of the LORD and from the treasuries of the king's palace. That's what he sent to the king of Assyria. I'd love to see a chariot in a gift box, though. I'd need a bigger box than any cookie box I've got.
Not this time, baker. Verse 9 says the king of Assyria took the people of Damascus to Kir as captives. They were not left in their city. Their city was captured and its people were carried off.
Nothing in the text says Uriah returns the plans, baker. Verse 11 says he built the altar according to all the instructions King Ahaz had sent. That's what he does with them in this verse.

Locking plans away isn't what verse 11 tells us, baker. Uriah the priest builds the altar according to all the instructions King Ahaz sent from Damascus. The verse says he built it, and it doesn't mention any locking away.

Right, baker. Verse 11 says Uriah completed the altar before King Ahaz returned. So when the king gets back, the altar is already finished. The text puts the finish line before the king's return, and that's all it says about timing.
It's actually true, friend. Uriah the priest completed the altar before King Ahaz returned from Damascus. Verse 11 says so plainly. So the king comes home to a finished altar.

You've got it. When the king came back from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and presented offerings on it (verse 12). Verse 13 then lists what he offered, starting with his burnt offering and his grain offering.
Ahaz is the one who sent the plans for this altar, baker, so tearing it down doesn't fit. Verse 12 says he approached it and presented offerings on it. That's what the king does with it.

Not this one, friend. Verse 12 says the king saw the altar, approached it and presented offerings on it. Moving it outside the city isn't mentioned. The moving comes later, in verse 14, and it's the bronze altar that Ahaz moves.

That's right, baker. Ahaz took the bronze altar that stood before the LORD and put it on the north side of the new altar. It had been standing between the new altar and the house of the LORD. So the bronze altar ends up on the north side of the new one.
The text shows no pushback, baker. Verse 16 says, “So Uriah the priest did just as King Ahaz had commanded.” That's all the verse tells us about his response.
This one's true, friend. Verse 17 says King Ahaz cut off the frames of the movable stands and removed the bronze basin from each of them. Then he went on to the Sea in the same verse.

Babylon, huh? Nice try, baker, but it never shows up in this chapter. The text says Ahaz removed the Sabbath canopy and closed the royal entryway on account of the king of Assyria. Assyria is who he'd been dealing with since verse 7. That king's name is all over this chapter, like flour on my apron.

Josiah did become king, friend. 2 Kings 22:1 says he was eight years old when he became king. The son who takes over from Ahaz, though, is Hezekiah. Good name, just not the one for this spot in the lineup.
